edits.content:
## Answer template (MANDATORY) and shape check
Before the answer tags write ONE short line, then the bare answer:
`Type: <noun the clue asks for> | Evidence: <quoted passage line, or own fact> | Check: <candidate put into the clue's blank reads correctly, is that kind of thing, is not a clue word, and fits one distinctive clue detail (team, number, size)>`
If the Check fails, choose a new candidate before answering. Then apply these shape rules to the final answer:
- HEAD NOUN OF 'this X' FIXES THE TYPE: 'a treaty signed in this Alpine city' -> the city, not the treaty; 'this caustic acid' -> the candidate must itself be an acid. If the filled-in blank is the wrong kind of thing, reject it.
- STRIP ECHOES: the answer never repeats a noun or phrase the clue already states, nor the clue's own 'this <noun>' label. Strike every clue word from the candidate and keep the remaining head: 'this vitamin' -> 'C' (not 'vitamin C'); 'A "hasty" dessert' -> 'pudding'; 'these exiles "of Poker Flat"' -> 'The Outcasts'; 'nicknamed this' (the Progressive party) -> 'Bull Moose' (not 'Bull Moose Party'); 'this funeral structure' -> 'Pyre'. 'One of these' with a common noun gets the plain noun, with no modifiers copied from passages. The Rule 4 head-noun exception applies only to slots like 'this empire' / 'this purchase', where the bare modifier alone cannot name the thing.
- CLUE ALREADY STATES PART OF A NAME ('this Beatle named Ringo', 'known by the first name Marilyn'): the answer is ONLY the missing part, not the full name. This overrides the 'first + last name' default.
- BARE 'TITLE + NAME' clue (only an office/ruler title plus a personal name, e.g. 'Prime Minister <Name>', 'Chancellor <Name>'): answer the ONE-WORD country, realm or organization that person heads. Take the country from the passages' 'X of <Country>' wording and give just the country. Never answer with a role phrase ('Queen of <Country>'), the title, or the name itself. A clue 'This <office>: "quote"' asks for the PERSON who said it (never a role phrase or a bare first name).
- 'these' / 'one of these' with named examples ('the oak & the maple are these'): answer the plain CATEGORY NOUN all the examples belong to ('Trees'), not a series, product set or exhibit named in a passage title.
- LIST OF CHARACTER NAMES (see Rule 1): answer the show/film/book TITLE shown in the passage headings, never a descriptive phrase that merely precedes the names.

edits.target: 'N-word' hints ('this 3-word phrase') work like a letter count: the answer must have exactly N words.
edits.content: - NOUN-PHRASE DEFINITION clues with no 'this' ('A tool for cutting grass'): the answer is the plain common term that paraphrases the WHOLE clue, found in a dictionary or thesaurus passage glossed with the clue's own words. Do not pick a narrower specialist or industry term just because it contains the clue's key word. If an archive line repeats the clue but its answer is cut off, use the dictionary/thesaurus entry that glosses the clue, not the archive page's topic words.

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content: - Match the NUMBER of the clue's noun phrase: a generic single object gets the singular ('Well', not 'wells'); a plural definition or 'these'/'ones'/a plural noun gets a plural answer; keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas'). Exception: a loanword or invariant noun whose passage headwords use the bare form (moose, sheep) stays bare, with no added -s.

edits.target: - Give only the MISSING part. If a word from the clue is part of the answer phrase, do not repeat it ('A "hasty" dessert' -> 'pudding', not 'hasty pudding'; 'Bridge to' this place -> 'Terabithia'). If the clue says 'this manicurist / this king / this dessert', do not append that role word to the answer.

- DELETE-CLUE-WORDS TEST: before answering, strike from your candidate every specific word or phrase the clue already states, and keep only the remaining head. 'Bret Harte wrote about these exiles "of Poker Flat"' -> 'The Outcasts' (not 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat'). 'Robert La Follette called it the Progressive party, but it was nicknamed this' -> 'Bull Moose' (not 'Bull Moose Party'). 'This funeral structure' -> 'Pyre' (not 'funeral pyre', and not 'funeral boat', which echoes the clue's 'funeral' and ignores that the passages say 'funeral pyre').
- 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - A bare quoted FILM / BOOK / ALBUM title with a year and no other words ('"Some Title"(1968)') asks for the PERSON who made it. Default to the director (or author or artist), the one passages credit as 'directed by' / 'written by', not a cast member named beside the title. Give the plain first + last name.

edits.target: - For nickname clues about a person ('known as "Uncle Walter"'), answer with the real name as it appears in the context (Walter Cronkite), not the nickname. Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content:
- Nickname clues: check the DIRECTION. If the clue gives the nickname ('known as "Uncle Walter"'), answer with the real name as it appears in the context (Walter Cronkite). If the clue gives the real name and asks for the 'moniker / nickname / better-known name', answer with ONLY the nickname word as the passages give it, not the real name and not nickname plus surname. Still apply the person-name rule when naming a real person.
- SPELLING AND WORDING: write names and terms in plain unaccented letters ('Zurich', not 'Zürich'), unless a verbatim archive answer (Rule 3) shows accents. For a common noun or term, use the exact wording that most passages and page titles use, not a synonym or variant from your own vocabulary.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - JOINT OR COMBINED ARTICLES: when a passage covers two people (an induction or 'versus' piece) and its stat line could belong to either, assign the facts using the clue's team, years and totals. The answer is the person whose OWN page (title or stats table with the same team and figures) carries the clue's exact numbers and team. A famous co-subject who played for a different team is wrong. Confirm the candidate belonged to the team the clue names.

edits.target: ## Rule 3: Look for the clue repeated verbatim in the context
edits.content: - Many clues begin with a host or video aside in parentheses ('(Jimmy of the Clue Crew ...)', '(Alex: We'll give you the horse...)'). Archives often store the aside separately from the clue body, so search on the distinctive words AFTER the aside, then copy the answer that follows the '|'.

edits.target: A phrase repeated across independent passages is strong evidence.
edits.content: - QUOTED-LINE clues: the quoted words are a search key, not the answer. (a) Cut-off line ('"...can change my complexion from white" to this color'): find passages printing the full line and copy exactly the words right after the cut-off, no more and no synonym. (b) Quote or poem/song/speech 'that begins "..."' about 'this <type>': if passages repeat the words but no answer is attached, read the neighbouring text, titles and tags for a named entity that fits the clue's descriptor, and answer with that entity's standard name, not the poem, the poet or the quote.

edits.target: - Archive lines may also be formatted 'CATEGORY | clue text | answer'. Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content: - A line like 'Jeopardy Question: CATEGORY - clue text.' may show the clue with no answer. Then look for a sibling passage that repeats the clue words (a Q&A page headed by the clue) and states the answer in its text. Answer with that entity in the name form the passages use.

edits.target: Give the bare name ('Ronald Reagan'), not the event, the place or the date.
edits.content: - BARE single-name clue (just 'Timonium', no 'this', no verb): every passage is about one small place, person or thing. Answer the larger entity the passages repeatedly tie it to under the usual category link. A town or neighbourhood -> its state or country, not the county, a business listed there, or a description. Confirm that most passages name the entity you chose.
